div.p: In the treatises I have already published on imitation, I went through the poets and prose writers whom I took to be the most distinguished, Quintus Aelius Tubero, and showed briefly what virtues each of them brings, both of substance and of style, and on what points each falls most short of himself in his failures, whether because his aim did not in every case pursue the most exact reckoning, or because his power did not succeed in all his works; my purpose being that those who set out to write and speak well might have fine and approved standards on which to base their particular exercises, not imitating everything that lies in those men, but taking their virtues and guarding against their failures. When I came to the historians, I set out my views about Thucydides too, but in a compressed and summary treatment — not out of contempt or indolence, nor for want of writers able to make good my contentions, but aiming at what was appropriate to the occasion of the work, as I did with the rest. For it was not possible to give an exact and detailed exposition of each of those men once I had chosen to compress the whole work into the smallest compass. But since you wished me to compose a separate treatise on Thucydides, embracing everything that requires discussion, I postponed the work on Demosthenes, which I had in hand, and promised to do as you preferred; and now, having fulfilled my promise, I deliver it.

As I am about to take up the discussion in detail, I wish to say a few preliminary words about myself and about the kind of work this is — not, by Zeus, for your sake and that of men like you, who judge matters from the standpoint of all that is best and hold nothing more precious than the truth, but for the sake of the others, in whom there is much fault-finding, whether it springs from emulation of the ancients, or from disdain of those of their own time, or from both of these passions together, which are common to human nature. For I suspect that there will be some among the readers of this work who will reproach me for daring to declare that Thucydides, the mightiest of all the historians, both sometimes errs in his choice of words and falls weak in his power. And this consideration occurred to me: that I shall be thought to be innovating paradoxes and to be the first and only man to do so, if I undertake to bring any charge against the writings of Thucydides — opposing not only the common opinions which all men, having received them from long ago, hold inalienably, but also disbelieving the particular testimonies of the most distinguished philosophers and orators, who set up that man as the standard of historical writing and the limit of skill in political oratory. Wishing, then, to clear myself of these reproaches, which have something theatrical about them and seductive to the many, I shall be content, about myself, to say only this much: that having all my life until now guarded against this contentious and quarrelsome temper, which barks at everyone without cause, and having published no work in which I accuse anyone — except one treatise that I composed in defense of political philosophy against those who unjustly run it down — I should not now, for the first time, set out to display against the most distinguished of the historians a malice that befits neither a free character nor my own habit. About the kind of work this is I had much to say, but I shall be content with a little. Whether I have chosen arguments that are true and proper to myself, you will judge, and so will every other lover of letters.

My intention in this work, then, is not an assault on the choices and powers of Thucydides, nor a reckoning up of his faults, nor a belittling of him, nor any other such undertaking, in which I should reckon his successes and virtues worth no mention but fasten upon what was not said in the best way. Rather it is a kind of accounting of the character of his style, embracing all that has fallen to him both in common with others and as distinctive beyond all the rest. In this it was necessary to speak not of his virtues only, but also of the vices that border upon them. For no human nature is so self-sufficient as to be without fault, whether in words or in deeds; the best is the one that succeeds most often and falls short least. Let each man, then, referring what is said to this premise, become not an accuser of my purpose, but a fair examiner of the particular features of his character. That I am not the first to undertake to do this, but that many, both of old and in our own day, have done so — not choosing quarrelsome writings but ones that contemplate the truth — though I could produce countless witnesses, I shall be content with two men alone, Aristotle and Plato. For Aristotle is not persuaded that everything was said in the best way by his teacher Plato — among which are the doctrines about the Idea, about the Good, and about the Republic; and Plato himself wishes to show that Parmenides and Protagoras and Zeno and not a few of the other natural philosophers were in error; and no one reproaches him on this very ground, considering that the aim of philosophical contemplation is the knowledge of the truth, from which the very end of life becomes clear. Now where no one blames those who differ about doctrines for their purpose, if they do not praise everything that belongs to their elders, would anyone surely blame those who have chosen to display the distinctive features of styles, if they do not attribute to their predecessors all the virtues — even those that do not belong to them?

One part of my defense still remains. It is an invidious charge, and gratifying to the many, but one that can easily be shown to be unsound. For it does not follow that because we fall short of Thucydides and the other men in power, we have therefore lost our capacity for judgment of them. Even those who do not possess the same skills as Apelles, Zeuxis, Protogenes, and the other famous painters are not thereby prevented from judging their arts, nor are those who are not such great craftsmen prevented from judging the works of Phidias, Polyclitus, and Myron. For I forbear to mention that of many works the layman is no worse a judge than the craftsman — of those, that is, which are grasped by the irrational sense and by the feelings — and that every art aims at these criteria and takes its starting point from them. But let me have done with prefaces, lest without noticing it I waste my discourse upon them.

As I am about to begin my treatise on Thucydides, I wish to say a few words about the other historians, both those older than he and those who flourished at the same time as he, from which both the choice of method by which he differed from his predecessors, and his power, will become clear. Many ancient historians, then, arose in many places before the Peloponnesian War, among whom are Eugeon of Samos, Deiochus of Proconnesus, Eudemus of Paros, Democles of Phygela, Hecataeus of Miletus, Acusilaus of Argos, Charon of Lampsacus, and Melesagoras of Chalcedon; and a little older than the Peloponnesian War, extending down to the age of Thucydides, were Hellanicus of Lesbos, Damastes of Sigeum, Xenomedes of Chios, Xanthus of Lydia, and many others. These men used a similar method in their choice of subjects, and had powers that did not differ much from one another, some recording Greek histories, others foreign ones; and these histories they did not connect with one another, but divided them by nations and by cities and brought them out separately, keeping one and the same aim: to bring out into the common knowledge of all, just as they had received them, whatever records were preserved among the local peoples, nation by nation and city by city, whether writings stored up in sacred places or in profane ones, neither adding anything to them nor taking anything away. Among these there were also certain legends believed from far-off time, and certain theatrical reversals of fortune which seem to people of today to have much that is silly. And as for style, they all for the most part practiced the same — those, that is, who chose the same character of the dialects — clear, common, pure, concise, suited to the subject matter, and displaying no artificial elaboration. Nonetheless a certain bloom and grace runs over their works, in some more, in others less, on account of which their writings still survive. But Herodotus of Halicarnassus, who was born a little before the Persian Wars and lived on until the Peloponnesian, carried the historian's purpose to greater scope and more splendor: choosing to record the history not of a single city nor of a single nation, but gathering many and various deeds from Europe and from Asia into the compass of a single work. For having begun from the empire of the Lydians, he brought his history down to the Persian War, embracing in one composition all the notable deeds done by Greeks and barbarians in two hundred and twenty years; and he restored to his style the virtues that had been left out by the historians before him.

Coming after these men, Thucydides chose neither to set his history in a single place, as Hellanicus and his school did, nor to gather into one history the deeds done in every land by Greeks and barbarians, imitating Herodotus; the former he disdained as cheap and lowly and not able to benefit the readers in many ways, the latter as too great to fall within the survey of human reckoning according to the most exact method. Rather, taking up a single war, the one the Athenians and Peloponnesians waged against one another, this he set himself to record — being strong in body and sound in mind and having lived through the whole of it, and not composing the events from chance reports, but, where he himself was present, from experience, and where he was absent because of his exile, learning from those who had the best knowledge. First, then, he differed from his predecessors in this — I mean in taking a subject neither wholly of a single strand nor divided into many disconnected headings; next, in not attaching to it anything legendary, nor turning his writing into the deceiving and bewitching of the many, as all his predecessors did, recording certain Lamiae rising from the earth in woods and glens, and amphibious Naiads coming up out of Tartarus, swimming through the sea and half beast, and these coming into intercourse with men, and from unions of mortals and gods offspring that were demigods, and other such tales incredible to our way of life and seeming to have much that is foolish in them.

I have been led to say this not in censure of those men, but rather with much indulgence toward them, if they did lay hold of legendary fictions in bringing out national and local histories. For among all men, both in common by regions and severally by cities, certain records of such tales too were preserved, as I said, which children, receiving them from their fathers, took pains to hand down to their descendants; and those who wished to bring them out for the public they expected to write down just as they had received them from the ancients. For those men, then, it was necessary to variegate their local records with legendary episodes. But for Thucydides, who chose a single subject, at which he himself was present, it was not fitting to mingle theatrical enchantments into his narrative, nor to adapt himself to the deception of his readers, which those compositions are by nature fitted to bring, but to their benefit, as he himself has shown in the preface to his history, writing word for word thus: "And as for hearing, the absence of the legendary in them will perhaps appear less pleasing. But whoever shall wish to examine the truth of what has happened and of what will one day, in the course of human things, be such or similar again, will find it enough to judge these things useful. They are composed as a possession for all time rather than as a prize-piece to be heard for the moment."

It is testified to the man, perhaps by all philosophers and orators, or if not by all, at least by most, that he took the greatest care for the truth too, of which we wish history to be the priestess, neither adding to the facts anything that was not just nor taking anything away, nor taking license in his writing, but keeping his purpose blameless and pure of all envy and all flattery, and most of all in his judgments about good men. For having mentioned Themistocles in the first book, he went over the virtues he possessed ungrudgingly; and when he touched on the policies of Pericles in the second book, he uttered a eulogy worthy of the renown that is famed of him; and concerning Demosthenes the general, and Nicias the son of Niceratus, and Alcibiades the son of Clinias, and other generals and orators, being compelled to speak, he set out what was fitting to each. But I have no need to bring forward examples about these things to those who have gone through his histories. These, then, are the things one may say in which the historian succeeds in the matter of substance — fine and worthy of imitation.

But the things he constructed more defectively, and on which some bring charges against him, belong to the more technical part of the substance, what is called the management of material, which is sought in all writings, whether one chooses philosophical subjects or rhetorical ones. These are the matters of division, of arrangement, and of working out. I shall begin from division, premising that, whereas the historians before him divided their records either by places or by easily followed times, he approved neither of these divisions. For he neither divided his narratives following the places in which the events were accomplished, as Herodotus and Hellanicus and certain others of his predecessors did, nor following the times, as those who brought out local history chose to do, dividing their records either by the successions of kings, or of priests, or by the cycles of the Olympiads, or by the magistrates appointed to the annual offices. Rather, wishing to travel a new and untrodden road, untrodden by the others, he divided his history by following the summer and winter seasons. But from this the opposite of what he expected has happened to him. For the division of the times has not become clearer but harder to follow. On which account it is worth wondering how it escaped him that, when many things happen at once in many places, a narrative crumbled into small sections will not catch that far-shining and pure light, as becomes clear from the events themselves. At any rate, in the third book — for with this alone I shall be content — having begun to write the affairs of Mytilene, before he has filled out the whole narrative, he goes off to the deeds of the Lacedaemonians; and not even bringing these to a head, he mentions the siege of Plataea; and leaving this too unfinished, he mentions the Mytilenean war; then from there he leads the narrative to the affairs of Corcyra, how they fell into faction, some calling in the Lacedaemonians, others the Athenians; and leaving these too half-done, he says a little about the earlier Athenian expedition to Sicily. Then, having begun to tell of the Athenian voyage against the Peloponnese and the Lacedaemonian expedition against the Dorians, he passes on to the things done at Leucas by Demosthenes the general and to the war against the Aetolians; and from there he goes off to Naupactus. Leaving the wars on the mainland unfinished too, he again takes up Sicily, and after this purifies Delos, and Amphilochian Argos, warred upon by the Ambraciots . . . he leaves. And why need I say more? For the whole book is so chopped up and has destroyed the continuity of the narration. We wander, then, as is natural, and follow what is set forth with difficulty, the mind being confused by the tearing apart of events, and not easily or exactly recalling the half-finished memories of what was heard. But historical writing ought to be continuous and undistracted, especially when it concerns many events and hard ones to learn. That this canon is not correct nor proper to history is clear. For none of the later historians divided his history by summers and winters; rather all followed the well-worn roads that can lead to clarity.

Some find fault also with his arrangement, on the ground that he neither took for his history the beginning he ought to have, nor fitted to it a fitting end, saying that it is no small part of good management both to take a beginning before which nothing could come, and to embrace the work with an end that will seem to leave nothing wanting; whereas of neither of these did he take the proper care. And the historian himself has furnished them the starting point of this accusation. For having declared at the outset that the Peloponnesian War was the greatest of the wars before it, both in length of time and in the conjunction of many sufferings, he wishes at the end of the preface to state first the causes from which it took its beginning. Laying down these as two — the true one, but not spoken of openly, the growth of the city of the Athenians, and the not true one, fabricated by the Lacedaemonians, the alliance sent from Athens to the Corcyraeans against the Corinthians — he has made the beginning of his narrative not from the true one, and the one he himself thinks true, but from the other, writing word for word thus: "The Athenians and Peloponnesians began it by breaking the thirty-years' truce that had been made between them after the capture of Euboea. And as to why they broke it, I have first written down the causes and the disputes, that no one may ever have to inquire from what such a great war arose among the Greeks. For the truest cause, though least spoken of in word, I consider to be that the Athenians, becoming great and offering fear to the Lacedaemonians, compelled them to go to war. But the causes openly alleged on each side were these. Epidamnus is a city on the right as one sails into the Ionian gulf. Bordering on it dwell the Taulantians, a barbarian people, an Illyrian nation." And after this he goes through the affairs of Epidamnus and of Corcyra and of Potidaea, and the assembly of the Peloponnesians at Sparta and the speeches delivered there against the city of the Athenians. Having drawn these out to as many as two thousand lines, then he renders his account of the other cause, the true one and the one he himself thinks true, beginning from here: "The Lacedaemonians voted that the truce had been broken and that they must war upon the Athenians, not so much persuaded by the speeches of the allies as fearing the Athenians, lest they grow more powerful, seeing that most of Greece was already subject to them. For the Athenians came to their power in this manner, by which they grew." To which he adds the deeds of the city, all that they accomplished after the Persian War down to the Peloponnesian, summarily and cursorily, in fewer than five hundred lines. And recalling that these were earlier than the Corcyrean affairs, and that the war took its beginning not from those but from these, he again writes, word for word, thus: "After these things there now come about, not many years later, the things mentioned before, the Corcyrean and Potidaean affairs and all that became the alleged cause of this war. And all these things that the Greeks did, both against one another and against the barbarian, came about in some fifty years between the withdrawal of Xerxes and the beginning of this war; in which the Athenians established their empire more firmly and themselves advanced to great power, while the Lacedaemonians, perceiving it, did not prevent it, except for a short time, but kept quiet for most of the period, being even before this slow to go to war unless compelled, and at that time also somewhat hindered by wars of their own — until the power of the Athenians plainly rose and laid hold of their alliance. Then at last they no longer found it endurable, but thought they must set to with all eagerness and bring down their strength, if they could, by taking up this war."

He ought, having begun to inquire into the causes of the war, to have rendered first the true one and the one he himself thought true. For nature demanded that the earlier things should come before the later, and that the true should be told before the false; and the opening of the narrative would have become far better had it met with such management. Nor indeed could anyone who wishes to defend him say that the matters were small and not worth mentioning, or common and worn out by his predecessors, so that there was no need to make a beginning from them. For he himself reckoned that this subject, as left out by the ancients, was worthy of history, writing in these very words: "I have written these things and made this digression because for all before me this ground was a gap: they composed either the Greek affairs before the Persian Wars or the Persian Wars themselves. And of these matters, the very ones Hellanicus touched on in his Attic history, he made mention briefly and with no exactness as to the times; and at the same time it contains a demonstration of the empire of the Athenians, in what manner it was established."

This, then, was sufficient proof that the narrative was not managed by him in the best way — I mean the fact that it does not have its natural beginning. There is added to this also the fact that the history did not end at the headings at which it ought. For though the war embraced twenty-seven years, and though he lived through all this time down to its conclusion, he brought his history down only to the twenty-second year, extending the eighth book to the sea-battle at Cynossema — and this though he had said in the preface that he would embrace all that was done in this war. And in the fifth book again he sums up the times, from when it began and down to where, having advanced, it was brought to an end, having written this word for word: "And to those who relied at all on oracles, this one alone turned out securely. For I always remember that, both at the beginning of the war and down to its end, it was repeatedly brought forward by many that it must last thrice nine years. I lived through the whole of it, perceiving with my age and applying my mind, that I might know something exactly; and it befell me to be in exile from my own country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis, and being present at the affairs on both sides, and not least with the Peloponnesians by reason of my exile, to perceive something of them the more at my leisure. The difference and confusion of the truce after the ten years, then, and the subsequent course of the war, I shall set forth."

That he is also less careful in the working out of the headings — either rendering more words than is needed for those that require fewer, or running rather carelessly over those that require more working out — though I could confirm it with many proofs, I shall use a few. The first two sea-battles of the Athenians and Peloponnesians, in which against forty-seven ships of the Peloponnesians the Athenians, with twenty ships alone . . . having fought at sea against many times their number of the barbarians, destroyed some and took others, men and all, no fewer than they had sent out to the war — these he began to write near the end of the second book. I shall set down his words: "After this there came about, on the Eurymedon river in Pamphylia, an infantry battle and a sea-battle of the Athenians and their allies against the Medes; and the Athenians conquered in both on the same day, Cimon the son of Miltiades being general, and they took the triremes of the Phoenicians and destroyed them, in all two hundred." Like to this in his work are also the infantry battles, either drawn out beyond what is needed or compressed below the proper measure. The affairs of the Athenians at Pylos and around the island called Sphacteria, in which, having shut up the Lacedaemonians, they reduced them by siege — these he began to recount in the fourth book; and having narrated by the way certain other deeds of this war between, then turning back again to the rendering of what follows, he went through everything done in the battles by both sides exactly and ably, himself assigning more than three hundred lines to the battles, and that though neither the slain nor those who gave up their arms were many. He himself, at any rate, summing up the affair of the battle, writes word for word thus: "There died on the island and were taken alive thus many. Four hundred and twenty hoplites in all crossed over; of these two hundred and ninety-two were brought back alive, and the rest died. And of these the Spartiates among the living were a hundred and twenty; and of the Athenians not many were killed."

But when he mentions the command of Nicias, when, taking with him sixty ships and two thousand Athenian hoplites, he sailed against the Peloponnese, and shutting up the Lacedaemonians in their forts, reduced by siege the Aeginetans dwelling in Cythera and in Thyrea, and ravaged much of the rest of the Peloponnese, from which he sailed back to Athens bringing a multitude of captives — these he has told cursorily, about the affairs in Cythera thus: "And a battle taking place, the Cytherians held out for a little while; then turning, they fled to the upper city, and later came to terms with Nicias and his fellow-commanders, to entrust themselves to the Athenians, saving their lives." And about the capture of the Aeginetans in Thyrea thus: "Meanwhile the Athenians, putting in and advancing at once with their whole army, take Thyrea, and burned the city and plundered what was in it, and the Aeginetans, all who were not killed in hand-to-hand fighting, they brought with them and came to Athens." But when great misfortunes befell both cities right at the beginning of the war, on account of which both came to desire peace — about the earlier, when the Athenians, their land cut up and their city ruined by the plague, despairing of all other help, sent an embassy to Sparta begging to obtain peace — he has neither named the men sent, nor the speeches delivered there by them, nor those who opposed them, by whom the Lacedaemonians, persuaded, voted down the reconciliation; but somehow he has told these things cheaply and carelessly, as of small and inglorious matters: "And after the second invasion of the Peloponnesians the Athenians, as their land had been cut up a second time and the disease pressed on them along with the war, were altered in their resolves, and held Pericles to blame as having persuaded them to make war and as the cause through whom they had fallen into their misfortunes; and they were set on coming to terms with the Lacedaemonians, and sending some envoys to them, they accomplished nothing." But about the later one, when the Lacedaemonians, setting out to recover the three hundred captured at Pylos, sent an embassy to Athens, he has both told the speeches delivered then by the Lacedaemonian and gone over the causes on account of which the truce was not concluded.

If, then, in the case of the Athenian embassy the exposition embracing the headings of what happened was enough, and there was no need of the speeches and exhortations the envoys used, the Lacedaemonians being neither persuaded nor accepting the truce, why on earth did he not keep the same procedure in the case of those who came from Sparta to Athens? For neither did those go away having accomplished the peace. But if these things had to be told exactly, why did he carelessly leave out the others? For surely he was not prevented by weakness of power from finding and setting out the available arguments about both. But if for some reason he chose to work out the one embassy, I cannot conjecture on what ground he preferred the Laconian to the Attic — the later in time instead of the earlier, the foreign instead of his own, the one that arose over lesser ills instead of the one over greater. Captures of cities and their razing and enslavements and other such misfortunes, which he is often compelled to write, he sometimes makes to appear so cruel and dreadful and worthy of pity in their sufferings that he leaves no room for excess to historians or to poets; and sometimes so lowly and small that not even a token of the dreadful falls upon the perception of those who read the man. As for what he has said about the city of the Plataeans, and about that of the Mytileneans, and about that of the Melians, I have no need to bring forward those passages in which from the height of his power he has worked out their misfortunes. But those in which he runs over and makes the sufferings small . . . in many places of the history — of these I shall make mention: "About these same times the Athenians, having reduced the Scionaeans by siege, killed the men of fighting age, enslaved the children and women, and gave the land to the Plataeans to occupy. And the Athenians, crossing again into Euboea with Pericles as general, subdued the whole of it; and the rest they settled by agreement, but the Hestiaeans they expelled and themselves held the land. And in this same period the Athenians removed the Aeginetans from Aegina, themselves and their wives and children, charging them with being not least to blame for the war against them; and Aegina, lying close to the Peloponnese, seemed safer for them to hold by sending out settlers of their own."

One might find many other things throughout the whole history that have either met with the highest working out, admitting neither addition nor subtraction, or are carelessly run over and have not even the slightest gleam of that famous force — most of all in the public speeches and in the dialogues and in the other rhetorical pieces. Foreseeing this, he seems to have left the history unfinished, as Cratippus too, who flourished at the same time as he and gathered up what was left out by him, has written, saying not only that these pieces became an obstacle to the deeds, but that they were also wearisome to the hearers. He says, at any rate, that the man himself, perceiving this, put down no rhetorical piece in the last parts of his history, though many things took place in Ionia, and many at Athens, that were done through dialogues and public speeches. If indeed one were to set the first and the eighth books side by side and compare them with one another, neither would they seem to be of the same purpose nor of the same power. For the one, embracing few and small matters, is full of rhetorical pieces; the other, composed about many and great deeds, is scant of public speeches.

I have indeed thought that, even in the rhetorical pieces themselves, this affliction has befallen the man: that on the same subject and at the same moment he sets down speeches that ought not, and leaves out those that ought, to be spoken. Such a thing he has done about the city of the Mytileneans in the third book. For after its capture and the arrival of the captives whom the general Paches sent, two assemblies taking place at Athens, the speeches delivered in the first by the demagogues — in which the people voted to kill the captives and the rest of the Mytileneans of fighting age, and to enslave the women and children — he left out as not necessary; but the speeches delivered in the second by the same men — in which a certain repentance came over the many — composed on the same subject, he took in as necessary.

And the famous Funeral Oration, which he went through in the second book — by what reckoning, after all, does it lie in this place rather than in another? For if, in the great misfortunes of the city, in which many brave Athenians perished fighting, the customary laments over them ought to be spoken, or if, in the great successes, from which some signal renown or power came to the city, the dead ought to be honored with funeral praises — in what book, rather than in this one, would it have been fitting for the funeral oration to be spoken? For in this book the Athenians who fell in the first invasion of the Peloponnesians were altogether very few, and not even these had done any brilliant deed, as Thucydides himself writes. For having said of Pericles that he guarded the city and kept it as quiet as he could — yet sent out some horsemen continually, that the scouts running ahead from the army might not work harm in the fields near the city — he says that a brief cavalry battle took place at Phrygii between one squadron of the Athenian horse, with the Thessalians on their side, and the horse of the Boeotians; in which the Thessalians and Athenians had the upper hand until, the hoplites coming to the aid of the Boeotians, there came a rout of them, and not many of the Thessalians and Athenians were killed; nevertheless they recovered them the same day without truce, and the Peloponnesians set up a trophy the next day. But in the fourth book the men with Demosthenes who fought at Pylos against the Lacedaemonian force both by land and by sea, and conquered in both battles, on account of whom the city was filled with boasting, were far more and braver than those. Why then, after all, does the historian open the public tombs for the few horsemen who won the city neither glory nor power, and bring on the most distinguished of the demagogues, Pericles, delivering that lofty tragic piece; but for the more and braver, on account of whom those who had carried the war against the Athenians fell beneath them, men fitter to obtain this honor, he did not compose the funeral oration? And — to let pass all the other battles, both by land and by sea, in which many perished who deserved far more justly to be adorned with funeral praises than the patrolmen of Attica, being ten or fifteen horsemen — those Athenians and their allies who died in Sicily with Nicias and Demosthenes, both in the sea-battles and in the struggles by land, and finally in the wretched flight, being no fewer than forty thousand and not even able to obtain the customary burial — how much fitter were they to obtain laments and funeral adornments? But he has so neglected these men that he has not even said this much: that the city set forth public mourning and performed the customary rites of the dead for those who had died on foreign soil, and appointed to speak over them the man who of the orators of that time was most able to speak. For surely it was not likely that the Athenians should publicly mourn over the fifteen horsemen, but think those who fell in Sicily — among whom more than five thousand of those on the muster-roll perished — worthy of no honor. But it seems that the historian — for I shall say what I think — wishing to make use of the person of Pericles and to compose the funeral praise as spoken by him, since the man died in the second year of this war and was present at none of the later misfortunes of the city, laid up, for that small and unimportant action, the praise that was above the worth of the matter.

One might see still more the unevenness of the historian in his working out, considering that, having left out many great matters, he draws out the preface of his history to as many as five hundred lines, wishing to show that the deeds done by the Greeks before this war were small and not worth comparing with it. For neither was the truth so, as may be shown from many things, nor does the principle of art prescribe to manage one's heightenings in this way — for it is not the case that, if something is greater than the small, it is therefore already great, but rather if it surpasses the great; and his preface, having taken so many demonstrative workings-out of his thesis, has become a history all by itself. But those who composed the rhetorical handbooks prescribe making prefaces samples of the speeches, anticipating the very headings of what is to be set forth. This, indeed, the man has done at the end of the preface, when about to begin the narrative, in fewer than fifty lines; so that all those many things that pull down the greatness of Greece were dragged in by him unnecessarily — that at the time of the Trojan War the whole was not yet called by one name "Greece," and that those who lacked sustenance began to cross by ship against one another, and falling upon unwalled cities inhabited village by village, plundered them and from this made the greatest part of their living. And what need was there to speak about the Athenians' luxury, which they used in old times — that they bound up topknots and wore golden cicadas in their hair? And that the Lacedaemonians were the first to strip naked and, undressing openly, to anoint themselves with oil along with their exercising? And the Corinthian shipwright Ameinocles who first built four triremes for the Samians, and Polycrates the tyrant of Samos who took Rheneia and dedicated it to the Delian Apollo, and the Phocaeans who founded Massalia and conquered the Carthaginians in a sea-battle, and all the other things like these — what occasion had they to be spoken before the narrative? But if it is lawful and permitted me to say what I think,

it seems to me the preface would have become best if he had fitted its last part to his thesis, leaving out all that lies between, and constructed it in this way: "Thucydides the Athenian wrote up the war of the Peloponnesians and Athenians, how they made war against one another, beginning right at its outset and expecting that it would be great and the most worthy of record of all that had gone before; reckoning from the fact that both were at the height of all preparation as it began, and seeing the rest of the Greek world taking sides with one or the other, some at once, some even intending to. For this was the greatest movement that came upon the Greeks and a certain part of the barbarians, and, one may say, upon most of mankind. For the things before these, and the still more ancient, it was impossible to discover clearly because of their lapse of time; but from the evidence in which, examining as far back as possible, I happen to put my trust, I do not think they were great, either in their wars or in other things. Neither do I trust rather to the poets, who have hymned of them, adorning them toward the greater, nor to the prose chroniclers, who composed toward what is more attractive to the hearing than truer, the things being unverifiable and most of them, through time, having prevailed incredibly into the legendary; but I reckon them to have been found out from the most signal evidences, as being adequately ancient. And this war, although men, in whichever war they are engaged, always judge the present one to be the greatest, but when they have ceased rather wonder at the ancient things — nevertheless from the deeds themselves, to those who examine them, will show itself to have been greater than they. And all that each side said in speech, either when about to go to war or already engaged in it, it was hard to remember the exactness of what was said, both for me, in the case of what I myself heard, and for those reporting to me from elsewhere; but as each seemed to me likely to say what was most needful about the matters in hand, keeping as close as possible to the whole sense of what was truly said, so it has been set forth. As for the deeds of what was done in the war, I did not think it right to write them down from any chance source, nor as seemed good to me, but having gone over those at which I myself was present, and those from others, with as much exactness as possible about each. They were found out with labor, because those present at the deeds did not say the same things about the same matters, but as each was disposed in goodwill or memory toward one side or the other. And for hearing, perhaps the absence of the legendary in them will appear less pleasing; but whoever shall wish to examine the truth of what has happened and of what will one day again, in the course of human things, be such or similar, will find it enough to judge these things useful. They are composed as a possession for all time rather than as a prize-piece to be heard for the moment. Of earlier deeds the greatest accomplished was the Persian War; and yet even this had its decision in two sea-battles and two land-battles. But of this war the length advanced far, and sufferings befell Greece in it such as no others in an equal time. For never were so many cities taken and made desolate, some by barbarians, some by the warring parties themselves, and there are some that even changed their inhabitants on being captured; nor so many flights of men and slaughter, some in the war itself, some through faction. And the things told before by hearsay, but more rarely confirmed in fact, became not incredible — about earthquakes, which prevailed over the greatest part of the earth at once and were most violent; eclipses of the sun, which occurred more frequently than those remembered from earlier time; great droughts in some places, and from them famines; and that which did not least harm and destroyed a part, the plague-like disease — for all these set upon them together along with this war. And the Athenians and Peloponnesians began it by breaking the thirty-years' truce that had been made between them after the capture of Euboea. And as to why they broke it, I have first written down the causes and the disputes, that no one may ever have to inquire from what such a great war arose among the Greeks."

Such, then, are the historian's failures and successes in the matter of substance. Now the matters of style, in which his character is most plainly visible, I am about to speak of. It is perhaps necessary first to say something about this kind too: into how many parts style is naturally divided, and what virtues it embraces; then to show in what condition Thucydides received it from the historians before him, and what parts he, first of all men, made new, whether for the better or for the worse, hiding nothing.

That all style is divided into two first parts — into the choice of words, by which matters are made clear, and into the composition of the smaller and greater members; and that of these again each is divided into further parts — the choice of the elementary members (I mean nouns, verbs, and connectives) into the literal expression and the figurative; the composition into the phrases, the clauses, and the periods; and that to both of these (I mean both the simple, indivisible words and the composite ones made from them) belong the so-called figures; and that of the so-called virtues some are necessary and ought to be present in all discourse, while others are added on and, when the first are present, then receive their own force — all this has been said by many before. So there is no need for me to speak of them now, nor from what observations and precepts each of these virtues arises, though they are many; for these too have met with the most exact working out by others.

Which of them all the historians before Thucydides used, and which they touched on only slightly, I shall go through summarily, taking it up from the beginning, as I promised; for thus will one know the man's own character more exactly. The very ancient ones, known only from their names, what kind of style they practiced I cannot conjecture — whether the plain and unadorned, having nothing superfluous but the useful and necessary things themselves, or the pompous and dignified and elaborate, having taken on the added adornments. For the writings of most of them do not survive down to our times, nor are those that do survive trusted by all to be the work of those men — among which are the writings of Cadmus of Miletus, of Aristeas of Proconnesus, and the like. But those born before the Peloponnesian War, extending to the age of Thucydides, all for the most part had similar purposes, both those who chose the Ionic dialect, which at that time was most in flower, and those who chose the ancient Attic, which has small differences from the Ionic. For all these, as I said, were more concerned with the literal expression than the figurative, and took up the figurative as a kind of seasoning; and they all practiced a similar composition of words, the unadorned and unstudied; and not even in figuring their words and thoughts did they go far from the well-worn, common, and familiar dialect of all. So the style of all of them has the necessary virtues (for it is pure and clear and adequately concise, each preserving the proper character of its dialect); but the added virtues, by which most of all the orator's power becomes plain, it has neither all nor reaching to their height, but few and in small measure — I mean elevation and beauty of expression and dignity and magnificence; nor yet tension, nor weight, nor passion to rouse the mind, nor the vigorous, contending breath, from which is born what is called force — except in Herodotus alone. For he, in the choice of words and in the composition and in the variety of figures, surpassed the others by far, and prepared his prose to become like the best poetry for the sake of persuasion and of graces and of pleasure reaching its height; and of the greatest and most brilliant virtues, except for the contending ones, he left out none . . . among these — whether because he was not well suited to them by nature, or because for some reason he willingly disdained them as not fitting for histories. For the man neither uses many public speeches nor contending discourses, nor has he his strength in making the matters passionate and dreadful.

To this man, then, and to the others whom I mentioned before, Thucydides applied himself, and discerning what virtues each of them had, he first set himself to bring into historical writing a character all his own, one overlooked by all. In the choice of words he preferred the figurative, the glossarial, the archaic, and the strange expression instead of the common and familiar to the men of his time; in the composition of both the smaller and greater members he preferred the dignified, austere, compact, firm, and harsh — roughening the ears with the clashing of the letters — instead of the clear, soft, smoothed-out, and unresisting; and in the figures, in which most of all he wished to differ from his predecessors, he brought the greatest zeal. At any rate he spent the twenty-seven years of the war, from the beginning to the end, turning the eight books — which alone he left — up and down, and filing and chasing each single part of the expression; now making a clause out of a word, now drawing a clause together into a word; now bringing out the verbal idea nominally, again making the noun a verb, and reversing the uses of these very things, so that the noun becomes appellative and the appellative is expressed nominally; and the passive verbs active, the active passive; changing the natures of plurals and singulars and predicating these of one another; joining feminine to masculine and masculine to feminine and neuter to some of these, from which the natural sequence is led astray; turning the cases of nouns or participles now from the signifier to the signified, now from the signified to the signifier; and in the connective and prepositional particles, and still more in those that articulate the powers of words, taking license like a poet. Most of all one would find in him figures altered from the customary by turnings of person and changes of tense and transferences of figurative significations, taking on the appearance of solecisms; and as many as occur of things in place of bodies or bodies in place of things; and those reflections and thoughts in which the parenthetic insertions, becoming many, carry their sequence at a long distance; and the crooked and complicated and hard-to-unravel constructions and the other things akin to these. One would find also not a few of the theatrical figures lying in his work — I mean the parisoses, the paromoioses, the paronomasias, and the antitheses — in which Gorgias of Leontini was excessive, and Polus and Licymnius and many others who flourished at the same time as he. And his most evident and characteristic feature is the attempt to signify the most matters through the fewest words, and to compose many thoughts into one, and to leave the hearer still expecting to hear something more — from which his brevity becomes obscure. But to speak summarily, there are, as it were, four instruments of the style of Thucydides: the poetic quality of the words, the variety of the figures, the harshness of the harmony, the swiftness of the significations; and its colors are the compact and the dense, the bitter and the austere, the weighty and the dreadful and the fearsome, and above all these the passionate. Such, then, is Thucydides in the character of his style, by which he differed from the others. When, accordingly, both his purpose and his power run out together, his successes become perfect and superhuman; but when his power falls short, the tension not holding to the end, then through the swiftness of the narration his style becomes obscure and brings on certain other unbecoming blemishes. For the question in what manner the strange and coined words ought to be used, and how far they should advance before stopping — fine and necessary observations in all works — he does not keep throughout the whole history.

These things having been said summarily, it is time to turn to the demonstrations of them. I shall make my discourse not separately about each kind of style, subordinating to them the language of Thucydides, but by certain passages and places, taking parts both of the narrative and of the rhetorical pieces, and setting beside the successes or failures, of substance and of style, the causes on account of which they are such; asking you again, and the other lovers of letters who will meet with this writing, to consider the intention of the subject I have chosen to examine, namely that it is a display of his character, embracing all that has fallen to him and requires discussion, having for its aim the benefit of those who shall wish to imitate the man. At the beginning of the preface, then, having used the proposition that the Peloponnesian War became the greatest of the wars before it, he writes word for word thus: "For the things before these and the still more ancient it was impossible to discover clearly because of their lapse of time; but from the evidence in which, examining as far back as possible, it befell me to put my trust, I do not think they were great, either in their wars or in other things. For the land now called Greece appears not to have been securely inhabited of old, but there were migrations in the earlier time, and each people readily abandoned its own, forced out by others always more numerous. For there being no commerce, nor mingling fearlessly with one another either by land or by sea, and each occupying their own only so far as to live off it, and having no surplus of wealth nor planting the land . . . enslaved in resolve as against the Lacedaemonians. Despising them, then, and shouting all together, they rushed upon them." This passage ought to have been constructed by him not in this way, but more in the common manner and more usefully, with the last member added to the first, and the things between taking the place after these. The expression, figured in this way, has become more crabbed and more forceful; but it would have been clearer and more pleasant constructed in that other way: "And the Lacedaemonians no longer being able to dart out where they were attacked, the light troops, perceiving them now slower, gathering together and shouting, rushed upon them all together, having taken on confidence from the sight, that they were many times their number, and despising them, since they no longer appeared as dreadful to them as before, because they had not at once suffered things answering to their expectation — the supposition they had held, when they first landed, enslaved in resolve as against the Lacedaemonians."

The whole passage being set aside, everything else has been named with the most fitting words and embraced with the most suitable figures, and has fallen short of no virtue, one may say, either of style or of substance — which I have no need to enumerate again. But in the seventh book, narrating the last sea-battle of the Athenians and Syracusans, he has named and figured the events thus: "Demosthenes and Menander and Euthydemus — for these went aboard the ships of the Athenians as generals — putting out from their own camp, sailed at once against the boom of the harbor and the gap that had been left, wishing to force their way out. But the Syracusans and their allies, having already put out with ships nearly equal in number to before, kept guard both at the exit with a part of them and around the rest of the harbor in a circle, so that they might fall upon the Athenians from all sides at once; and their infantry came to their aid wherever the ships put in. The commanders of the Syracusan fleet were Sicanus and Agatharchus, each holding a wing of the whole, and Pythen and the Corinthians the center. When the rest of the Athenians too came up against the boom, by their first onset, sailing on, they overpowered the ships drawn up against it and tried to loose the fastenings; but after this, the Syracusans and their allies bearing down on them from all sides, the sea-battle came to be no longer at the boom only, but throughout the harbor; and it was fierce, and such as no other before. For there was much eagerness on each side, on the part of the sailors, to sail on whenever the order was given, and much counter-skill of the helmsmen and contention with one another; and the marines took care, whenever ship fell upon ship, that the work from the deck should not fall short of the rest of the art; and every man, in the post to which he had been assigned, hastened himself to appear first. And many ships falling together in a narrow space — for these were the most that ever fought in a narrow space, for the two sides fell little short of being two hundred — the backings-out were few, because there was no room for backing water and breaking through; but the onsets were more frequent, as it chanced that ship fell upon ship, either in flight or sailing against another. And as long as a ship was bearing down, those from the decks used javelins and arrows and stones against it in plenty; but when they came alongside, the marines, coming to hand-strokes, tried to board one another's ships. And it happened in many places, because of the narrowness, that some had rammed others and others were themselves rammed, and that two ships, and in some cases more, were perforce entangled about one; and that for the helmsmen there was, of some ships defense, of others attack — not against each single one, but against many from all sides at once — and that the great crash from many ships falling together caused both consternation and deprivation of hearing of what the boatswains shouted. For there was much exhortation and shouting from the boatswains on either side, both by their art and in the naval rivalry: to the Athenians they shouted to force the passage out and now, if ever, eagerly to lay hold of safe return to their fatherland; to the Syracusans and their allies, that it was a fine thing to prevent them from escaping and, each conquering, to exalt his own fatherland. And the generals on each side, besides, if they saw any backing water anywhere without necessity, calling the trierarch by name, asked — the Athenians, whether they were withdrawing because they now thought the most hostile land more their own than the sea they had won with no small toil; the Syracusans, whether they, who clearly knew the Athenians eager in every way to escape, were themselves fleeing the fleers. And the infantry on land of both sides, the sea-battle standing balanced, had much struggle and tension of mind: the man from home, contending now for the greater glory; the invaders fearing that they might fare even worse than the present. For all the Athenians' fortunes being staked on the ships, their fear for the future was like nothing, and because of the unevenness they were forced to have the view of the sea-battle from the land an uneven one too; for, the spectacle being at close range and not all looking at the same point at once, if any saw their own men prevailing somewhere, they took heart and turned to call upon the gods not to deprive them of safety; but those who looked toward the part being beaten used lamentation along with shouting, and from the sight of what was done were more enslaved in mind than those in the action; and others, looking toward a part of the battle that was even, because of the uninterrupted continuity of the contest, swaying in terror with their very bodies in time with their thought, passed the most grievous of times; for always they were within a little either of escaping or of being destroyed. And there was in the army of the Athenians, as long as the sea-battle was nearly equal, everything to be heard at once — lamentation, shouting, 'we win, we are beaten,' and all the other manifold things a great army is forced to utter in great danger. And like things to these the men on the ships also suffered, until at last the Syracusans and their allies, the sea-battle having long held out, turned the Athenians and, pressing on splendidly with much crying and cheering, pursued them to the land. Then indeed the naval host, those who had not been taken on the open water, carried in one here, one there, fell out upon the camp. And the infantry, no longer divided, but with one impulse, with wailing and groaning, all hard put to bear what was happening, some ran to the aid of the ships, others to the guard of what was left of the wall; while others, and now the most, were already looking out for themselves and how they should be saved. And in that instant there was a consternation second to none of all. They had suffered things like, and themselves done like, at Pylos; for, the ships of the Lacedaemonians being destroyed, the men on the island who had crossed over were lost to them besides. And now to the Athenians it was beyond hope to be saved by land, unless something should happen against reason. And the sea-battle having become violent and many ships and men being lost on both sides, the Syracusans and their allies, prevailing, took up the wrecks and the dead and, sailing back to the city, set up a trophy."

To me, then, these things and the like seemed worthy of emulation and imitation, and I was persuaded that the man's grandeur of speech and beauty of style and force and the other virtues are in these works most perfect — reckoning from the fact that every soul is led by this kind of style, and that neither the irrational criterion of the mind, by which we are naturally fitted to grasp the pleasant or the painful, is estranged from it, nor the rational, by which the beautiful in each art is discerned; and neither would those who are not at all experienced in political discourse be able to say at what word or figure they are vexed, nor would those who are quite refined and look down on the ignorance of the many be able to blame the construction of this style; but both the judgment of the many and that of the few will have the same supposition. For that great common layman will not be vexed at the vulgarity or crookedness or difficulty of the style; and the rare craftsman, one not made by any chance training, will not blame the ignoble and base and unwrought. Rather both the rational and the irrational criterion, by both of which we think all things should be judged in the arts, will be in concord. . . . [if it] should work the one, it no longer renders the other beautiful or perfect.

I, for my part, do not know how to praise those things that seem to some great and wonderful, which do not even have the first and most common virtues, but are so overcome by the elaborate and superfluous as to be neither pleasant nor useful; of which I shall furnish a few samples, setting beside each at once the causes on account of which it has fallen round into the vices opposite to the virtues. In the third book, then, going through the cruel and unholy deeds done at Corcyra, because of the faction, against the most powerful men from the people, as long as he sets forth what was done in the common and familiar manner of the dialect, he has said everything clearly and concisely and ably; but when he begins to make a tragedy of the common misfortunes of the Greeks and to alter his thought from what is customary, he becomes by a long way worse than himself. The first part, which no one would lay hold of as faulty, is this: "The Corcyraeans, perceiving the Attic ships sailing up and those of the enemy gone, took the Messenians, whom they brought into the city, having before been outside, and ordering the ships they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbor, in the while they were being conveyed round, killed any of their enemies they laid hold of, and bringing out of the ships all whom they had persuaded to embark, dispatched them. And going to the Heraeum, they persuaded about fifty men of the suppliants to submit to trial, and condemned all to death; but the many of the suppliants, all who had not been persuaded, when they saw what was happening, destroyed one another in the sanctuary, and some hanged themselves from the trees, and others made away with themselves each as he could. And for seven days, during which Eurymedon, having arrived with his sixty ships, remained, the Corcyraeans went on slaughtering those of their own whom they took to be enemies, bringing the charge against those who were subverting the democracy; but some died also for private enmities, and others on account of moneys owed them, at the hands of those who had borrowed. And every form of death came to pass, and, as is wont to happen in such circumstances, there was nothing that did not come about, and still further; for father killed son, and men were dragged from the sanctuaries and killed at them, and some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there. So cruelly did the faction advance; and it seemed the more so, because it was among the first to occur — since later, indeed, well-nigh the whole Greek world, one may say, was moved, there being everywhere differences, the leaders of the democracies calling in the Athenians, and the oligarchs the Lacedaemonians."

But what he adds to these is crooked and hard to follow, having figured combinations that look like solecisms, practiced neither by those who lived in his time nor by those later, when political eloquence most flourished — which I am now about to quote: "And so the affairs of the cities were in faction, and the things coming somewhat later, by the report of what had gone before, carried far the excess of innovating their resolves, both by the over-contriving of their attempts and by the strangeness of their reprisals." In these the first of the clauses is periphrased to no necessary purpose: "And so the affairs of the cities were in faction" — for it would have been sounder to say "and so the cities were in faction." And what is said next, "and the things coming somewhat later," is hard to make out; it would have become clearer if said thus: "and the cities that came later." To which is added: "by the report of what had gone before carried far the excess toward innovating their resolves" — for he wishes to say: "but those who came later, learning by inquiry what had been done among others, took on an excess toward devising something newer." And apart from the construction, not even the figurings of the words are pleasant to the ears. To these he adds another heading, more proper to poetic, or rather to dithyrambic, elaboration: "both by the over-contriving of their attempts and by the strangeness of their reprisals; and they exchanged the customary estimation of words, as applied to deeds, by their new justification." For what he wishes to make clear in this hard-to-unravel construction is this: "they took on a great increase toward devising something newer in the arts of their enterprises and in the excesses of their reprisals; and transferring the words customarily applied to matters, they thought fit to call them otherwise." But "the over-contriving" and "the strangeness of the reprisals" and "the customary estimation of words" and "the justification exchanged as applied to deeds" are more proper to poetic periphrasis. To these he adds these theatrical figures: "For unreasoning daring was reckoned courage loyal to one's party, and provident delay specious cowardice." For both of these contain paromoioses and parisoses, and the epithets are set down for the sake of embellishment; for what is not theatrical . . . but a necessary figure of style would have been such as this: "for daring they called courage, and delay cowardice." Like to these are also the things joined to them: "and prudence the pretext of the unmanly, and intelligence toward everything inactivity toward all" — which would have been more properly said thus: "the prudent were unmanly, and the intelligent in all things inactive in all."

If, having advanced thus far, he had stopped — embellishing his style here, hardening it there — he would have been less wearisome. But as it is he adds: "and to have been plotting was safety, the pretext of escape reasonable; and the man who was harsh was always trustworthy, and the one who contradicted him suspect." For in these again it is unclear whom he wishes to indicate as the harsh man and about what, and whom as the contradicter and on what point. "He who has plotted," he says, "and succeeded was intelligent, and he who suspected still more clever; but he who took forethought so that he should have no need of either was a dissolver of his party and panic-stricken before his opponents." For neither does "he who has succeeded" reveal more what he wishes to make clear, nor can the same man be thought "having succeeded and having suspected" at once, if indeed "having succeeded" is said of one who has prospered and attained what he hoped, and "having suspected" of one who has foreseen the evil not yet done but still impending. The sense would have been pure and far-shining thus: "those who plotted against others, if they succeeded, were clever; and those who suspected the plots beforehand, if they guarded against them, still cleverer; but the man who foresaw so that he should have no need either of plotting or of guarding was reckoned both to dissolve the parties and to have panicked his opponents."

Adding to these one period crabbedly expressed, yet ably along with clearly: "And simply, the man who forestalled another about to do some evil was praised, and the man who urged on one not even minded to," he uses again a poetic transference: "and indeed kinship became more alien than party, because of being readier to dare without pretext." For "the kindred thing" and "the party thing," set down instead of "kinship" and "party," are transferred; and "to dare without pretext" is unclear, whether it is set down here of the friends or of the kindred. For having given the cause on account of which they judged the kindred more alien than the friends, he adds that "they offered daring without pretext." The discourse would have been clear if he had brought it out in this way, figuring it according to his own wish: "and indeed party became more proper than kinship, because of being readier to dare without pretext." And the things after these too are periphrased, and are reported neither forcefully nor clearly: "for such gatherings were not for the benefits of the established laws, but against the standing order, through greed." The sense is of this kind: "for the gatherings of the parties did not come about for the benefits according to law, but for grasping something contrary to the laws." And "oaths," he says, "if anywhere of reconciliation, given for the moment to each in his straits, held good, as they had no power from elsewhere." In these is hyperbaton and periphrasis; for "the oaths of reconciliation" have a signification of this kind: "the oaths concerning friendship, if anywhere they came about." And "held good," set by hyperbaton, follows "for the moment," for he wishes to make clear "they held for the present moment"; and "given to each in his straits, as they had no power from elsewhere" would have been clearer if brought out thus: "given to each in his straits because of having no other power." And the coherence of the thought would have been such as this: "the oaths concerning friendship, if anywhere they came about, given to each for want of any other pledge, held for the moment."

More crooked than these are the things he sets down after: "But in the chance opportunity, the one who first took courage, if he saw the other unguarded, took vengeance with more pleasure because of the trust than from the open way; and he reckoned both the safety, and that, getting the upper hand by deceit, he won besides a prize of intelligence." Now "the chance opportunity" is set instead of "on the instant," and "unguarded" instead of "off his guard"; and "taking vengeance with more pleasure because of the trust than from the open way" is darkly periphrased, and some member is lacking for the completion of the sense. One may guess that this is what he wishes to say: "but if at any time the occasion presented itself to anyone and he learned his enemy off his guard, he took vengeance with more pleasure, because he set upon one who trusted rather than one on his guard; and he won besides a reputation for intelligence, reckoning both the safety and that he got the better of him by the deceit." "And more easily," he says, "the many, being evildoers, are called clever than the unlearned good, and at the one they are ashamed, but at the other they exult." For these things are said crabbedly and briefly, and have their signification lying in obscurity. For it is hard to learn whom, after all, he means by "the unlearned and good"; for if he sets them in contrast to the evildoers, those who are not evil would not be unlearned; and if he sets "the unlearned" among the senseless and foolish, on what ground does he call these "good"? And "at the one they are ashamed" — who? For it is unclear whether both or the unlearned. And "at the other they exult" — here too it is unclear who; for if he sets it of both, it has no sense, for neither do the good exult at the evildoers nor are the evildoers ashamed at the unlearned.

This character of obscure and entangled style, in which there is more of the troublesome darkening of the thought than of charm, is drawn out to a hundred lines. I shall set down the rest too, no longer adding any word of my own: "Of all these the cause was rule arising from greed and ambition, and from these the eagerness of those settling into rivalry. For those who took the lead in the cities, each side with a specious name — the one of the equal political rights of the multitude, the other of a temperate aristocracy — while in word tending the common interest, made it their prize; and contending in every way to get the better of one another, they dared the most dreadful things, and pursued their reprisals to ones still greater, not setting their limit at what was just and beneficial to the city, but defining it by what at each time gratified each side; and whether by the condemnation of an unjust vote or by getting the mastery by main force, they were ready to glut their present rivalry. So that neither side practiced piety, but those to whom it befell to accomplish something invidious by a specious use of words were better thought of; and the citizens in the middle were destroyed by both, either because they would not join the contest, or out of envy that they should survive. Thus every form of bad character came to be established among the Greek world through the factions; and simplicity, of which the noble has the largest share, was laughed down and vanished; and to be set against one another in mind, distrustfully, prevailed far. For there was none to dissolve it, neither secure word nor fearful oath; but all, being superior in reckoning, in the hopelessness of anything secure, looked rather to suffering no harm than were able to trust. And the poorer in judgment, for the most part, prevailed. For, fearing both their own deficiency and the intelligence of their opponents, lest they should be inferior in words and be forestalled in being plotted against out of the versatility of their adversaries' wit, they went boldly to deeds; while the others, despising and thinking they would perceive beforehand, and that they need take in act nothing of what was possible by judgment, were destroyed the more unguarded." Though I could still make it clear from many examples that he is better in narratives, when he stays in the customary and common character of the dialect, and worse when he turns the dialect from the customary toward strange words and forced figures, some of which present the appearance of solecisms, I shall be content with these, that my writing may not advance beyond what is needed.

Since I promised to make clear my views also about his public speeches, in which some think the historian's power is at its height, having divided this examination too into two, the matter of substance and the matter of style, I shall discourse separately about each, beginning from the substance. In this the first part is the invention of the reflections and thoughts, the second the use of what is invented; the former having its strength rather in nature, the latter in art. Of these the one that has more of the natural than of the technical, and needs less teaching, is something wonderful in the historian; for he brings, as from a rich spring, an unmeasured store of thoughts and reflections, superfluous and strange and paradoxical. But the one that has more of the technical and makes the other appear more brilliant is in many places more deficient than is needed. Those, then, who have admired him beyond measure, as differing in nothing from the divinely inspired, seem to have suffered this affection because of the multitude of his reflections. If one teaches them, setting beside each matter the discourse, that these things were not suitable to be said at this moment and by these persons, and that those things were not suitable to these matters nor to this extent, they are vexed, suffering something like those who are conquered by the love of some beauty not far from madness. For those men think that all the virtues which belong to fair forms belong to the women who have enslaved them, and put forward as malicious and slanderers those who try to reproach them, if there is any blemish about them; and these critics, stupefied in mind by this one virtue, bear witness to the historian even of things that do not belong to him — for what each man wishes to be in the thing loved and admired by him, that he thinks it is. But those who keep their mind uncorrupted and refer the examination of discourse to the right standards, whether they have partaken of some natural judgment or have constructed strong criteria through teaching, neither praise everything equally nor are vexed at everything, but to the successes they render the fitting witness, and if some part has gone amiss in them, they do not praise it.

I, at any rate, who in all my observations lay down standards, neither shrank before from bringing my views into the open, nor now shall I turn aside from it. Granting, then, in the first place — as I said at the outset — the historian's good aim in invention, and supposing that, if anyone has supposed otherwise, whether through contentiousness or through dullness, thinking he errs, I no longer grant the other thing, his technical skill in the management of his material, except in very few public speeches. I see also the faults of style, about which I have already spoken, most and greatest befalling these kinds; for the glossarial, strange, and coined words abound most in these, and the complicated, crabbed, and forced figures are most about them. Whether I have judged what is reasonable, you will determine, and so will every other man led to the examination of the works. The setting of them side by side will be in the same manner, comparing those that seem to me best with those that are neither well managed nor blameless in expression.

In the second book, then, having begun to write of the march of the Lacedaemonians and their allies against Plataea, he lays down that, the king of the Lacedaemonians, Archidamus, being about to ravage the land, envoys came to him from the Plataeans; and he renders speeches such as were likely to have been spoken by both, fitting to the persons and proper to the matters and neither falling below the mean nor going above it, and has adorned them with a style pure and clear and concise and having the other virtues; and he has rendered the harmony so musical as to bear comparison with the most pleasant. "The following summer the Peloponnesians and their allies did not invade Attica, but marched against Plataea; Archidamus the son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, led them, and having encamped his army, he was about to ravage the land. But the Plataeans, sending envoys to him at once, spoke as follows: 'Archidamus and Lacedaemonians, you do what is neither just nor worthy of yourselves nor of the fathers from whom you are, in marching against the land of the Plataeans. For Pausanias the son of Cleombrotus, a Lacedaemonian, having freed Greece from the Medes together with the Greeks who were willing to share the danger of the battle that took place in our country, and having sacrificed in the market-place of the Plataeans victims to Zeus the Liberator, and having called together all the allies, restored to the Plataeans their land and city to hold and inhabit independent, and that no one should ever march unjustly against them or for enslavement; and if so, the allies then present should defend them with all their power. These things your fathers granted us for the sake of the valor and eagerness that were shown in those dangers. But you do the opposite of those men; for with the Thebans, our bitterest enemies, you have come for our enslavement. Calling to witness the gods who were then sworn by, and your own ancestral gods and our native ones, we tell you not to wrong the Plataean land nor to transgress the oaths, but to let us dwell independent, as Pausanias judged just.' When the Plataeans had said such things, Archidamus answered as follows: 'You speak justly, men of Plataea, if you do as your words say. For just as Pausanias delivered it over to you, be yourselves independent, and join in freeing the others, all who, having shared in the dangers of that time, both swore the oath with you and are now under the Athenians; for this great preparation and war have come about for their sake and the liberation of the rest. Of this, best of all, having yourselves a share, abide by the oaths; but if not, do what we have already before invited you to do — keep quiet, occupying your own; be of neither party, but receive both as friends, neither for war. And these things will satisfy us.' So much Archidamus said.
