And the envoys of the Plataeans, having heard these things, went into the city; and having communicated what was said to the multitude, they answered him that it was impossible for them to do what he invited without the Athenians; for their children and wives were with them. And they feared also for the whole city, lest, those having withdrawn, the Athenians coming should not allow them, or the Thebans, being included in the 'receiving both,' should again try to seize their city. But he, encouraging them in face of this, said: 'Hand over your city and houses to us the Lacedaemonians, and show the boundaries of your land, and your trees and whatever else can come to count; and remove yourselves wherever you wish, as long as the war lasts; and when it is over, we shall restore to you whatever we received; and until then we shall hold them as a deposit, working them and bearing a tribute that shall be sufficient for you.' And they, having heard this, again went into the city, and having deliberated with the multitude, said that they wished first to communicate to the Athenians what he invited, and if they persuaded them, to do it; and until then they bade him make a truce with them and not ravage the land. And he made a truce for as many days as it was likely the journey would take, and did not cut the land. And the Plataean envoys, having gone to the Athenians and deliberated with them, came back again announcing to those in the city the following: 'The Athenians say, men of Plataea, that neither in the time before, since we became allies, have they in anything given you up to be wronged, nor will they now overlook you, but will help you with all their power; and they adjure you by the oaths your fathers swore to make no innovation in the alliance.' When the envoys had reported such things, the Plataeans resolved not to betray the Athenians, but to endure, even seeing their land cut up, if need be, and suffering whatever else might come about; and that no one should go out any more, but should answer from the wall that it was impossible for them to do what the Lacedaemonians invited. And when they had answered, then for the first time Archidamus the king set himself to call to witness the gods and heroes of the country, saying thus: 'Gods, all who hold the land of Plataea, and heroes, be witnesses that neither in the beginning unjustly — but these having first abandoned the sworn agreement — did we come against this land, in which our fathers, having prayed to you, conquered the Medes, and you granted it gracious for the Greeks to contend in; nor now, if we do anything, shall we do wrong; for having invited them to many reasonable things, we do not obtain them. Be ye consenting that those who first began the wrong should be punished, and that those who bring vengeance lawfully should obtain it.' Having thus called the gods to witness, he set the army to war."

Let us examine, beside this dialogue so beautiful and admirable, another dialogue of his, which the admirers of this character most praise. He lays down that, the Athenians having sent an army against the Melians, colonists of the Lacedaemonians, before the war began the general of the Athenians and the magistrates of the Melians came together for discussion about ending the war; and at the start he makes clear, from his own person, what was said by both; but after a single answer, having kept this figure, the narrative one, he gives a personal cast to the dialogue that follows and dramatizes it. The Athenian begins, saying this: "Since the discourse is not made before the multitude, lest the people, hearing seductive and unrefuted things from us continuously in a single speech, be deceived at one hearing — for we know that this is the intent of our being brought before the few — you who sit here can make it still safer. Do not even you answer with a single set speech, but, against whatever does not seem to be said suitably, judge by taking us up at once. And first say whether what we propose pleases you." And the councillors of the Melians answered: "The fairness of teaching one another at leisure is not blamed; but the things of the war, present already and not impending, appear at variance with it." This last sentence, if anyone shall think fit to count among figures, would not be slow to call figures all the solecisms that occur against numbers and against cases. For having set forth "the fairness of teaching one another at leisure is not blamed," then having joined to the singular, brought out in the nominative case, "but the things of the war, present already and not impending," he yokes to these a word that is singular and figured in the genitive case — whether one wishes to call it a demonstrative article or a pronoun — namely "it"; and this, fitted neither to the feminine, singular, and nominative, preserves the sequence, nor to the plural, neuter, and figured in the accusative. The discourse would have been coherent figured thus: "the fairness of teaching one another at leisure is not blamed, but the things of the war, present already and not impending, appear at variance with her." To these he adds a reflection conceived not absurdly, but expressed in a way not easy to follow: "If, then, you have come together either to reckon up suspicions of what is to come, or anything else, than to take counsel for the safety of the city from the present things and from what you see, we stop; but if for this, we would speak."

And after this, turning the dialogue of the narrative to the dramatic, he makes the Athenian answer thus: "It is likely and pardonable that men set in such a condition should turn to many sayings and seemings." Then, having laid down a seemly proposition, "Nevertheless the meeting is present already and about safety; let the discourse, in the manner you propose, if it seems good, take place," first he has uttered a reflection neither worthy of the city of the Athenians nor fitting to be said on such matters: "We, then, for our part, will not, with fine words — that either we rule justly, having put down the Mede, or are now coming against you because we are wronged — furnish a length of discourse you would not believe." This is the act of one who admits the campaign against people who do no wrong, since he wishes to render no account of either of these. To which he adds: "Nor do we think it fitting that you, either because, being colonists of the Lacedaemonians, you did not join their campaign, or because you have done us no wrong, should think to persuade us by speaking; but that each side should accomplish what is possible according to what we both truly think." This means: "you, truly thinking that you are wronged, bear the necessity and yield; and we, not ignorant that we wrong you, by force will get the better of your weakness; for these things are possible for each side." Then, wishing to give the cause of this, he adds: "Because just things are judged, in human reckoning, from equal necessity; but the powerful do what is possible, and the weak yield."

For these things it was fitting for barbarian kings to say to Greeks; but for Athenians, against the Greeks whom they freed from the Medes, it was not proper to say that just things belong to equals among one another, but violent things to the strong against the weak. And the Melians having answered a little to this — that it would be well for the Athenians to take forethought for the just, lest one day they too, tripped up by others, fall into another's power and suffer the same at the hands of the stronger — he makes the Athenian answer: "But we, even if our empire be brought to an end, are not despondent about its ending"; giving as the cause that even if the Lacedaemonians should put down their empire, they will have indulgence, themselves doing many such things. I shall set down his words too: "For it is not those who rule over others, like the Lacedaemonians, who are dreadful to the conquered." This is like saying that among tyrants tyrants are not hated. To which he adds: "And about this let it be left to us to run the risk" — which a pirate or a brigand could scarcely have said — "I am not concerned about the vengeance afterward, having gratified appetites in the present." Then, a few exchanges between having occurred, and the Melians coming down to a fair proposal — "But that, keeping quiet, we should be friends instead of enemies, allies of neither — would you not accept?" — he makes the Athenian answer: "For your enmity does not harm us so much as your friendship — a proof of weakness to those we rule, while your hatred is a proof of power" — a wretched reflection, crookedly expressed; but if one wishes to consider its thought, it is of this kind: "loving us, you will make us appear weak to the others; hating us, strong; for we do not seek to rule by the goodwill of our subjects, but by fear."

Adding to these others again — laborious and bitter exchanges — he lays down the Melians saying that the enemy bear their fortunes in common, and that to yield at once is at once hopeless, but with action there is yet hope of standing upright. Against this he makes the Athenian answer things more crooked than labyrinths, about hope, which comes to men for their hurt, writing word for word thus: "And hope, being a comfort of danger, those who use it from a superabundance, even if it harm them, it has not cast down; but to those who stake it on all they have — for it is by nature prodigal — at once it is recognized when they have failed, and in the very point where one might guard against it, once it is known, it does not leave off. Which you, being weak and on a single throw, do not wish to suffer, nor to become like the many, to whom, while it is yet possible to be saved in a human way, when, hard pressed, the visible hopes leave them, betake themselves to the invisible — divination and oracles and all such things, which with hopes work ruin." These things I do not know how one could praise as fitting to be said by Athenian generals — that the hope from the gods works ruin to men, and that there is no use of oracles nor of divination to those who have chosen a pious and just life. For if anything, this too is among the first praises of the city of the Athenians: to follow the gods in every matter and at every season, and to accomplish nothing without divination and oracles. And the Melians saying that, with the help from the gods, they trust also in the Lacedaemonians, who, if for no other reason, at least for shame will help them and not overlook their kinsmen being destroyed, he brings on the Athenian answering still more arrogantly: "Of the favor of the divine we too do not think we shall fall short; for in nothing, beyond human wishes toward the divine and toward one another, do we claim or do anything. For we hold that the divine, by repute, and the human, clearly, always by a necessity of nature, rule wherever it has power." The sense of this is hard to conjecture even for those who seem very experienced in the man, but it is shut up to some such conclusion: that all men know the divine by repute, but judge what is just toward one another by the common law of nature; and this is to rule whatever one can master. These things too follow upon the first, and are fitting to be said by neither Athenians nor Greeks.

Though I could still furnish many sentiments that have a wicked cleverness, that my discourse may not become beyond measure, I shall take up only the last addition, which the Athenian spoke as he left the meeting: "But of your resources, the strong ones, being hoped for, are still to come; and the present ones are few to prevail over those already drawn up against you." "Much unreason of mind," he says, "do you display, if you will not, having removed us, resolve on something else more temperate than these things." To which he adds: "For surely you will not turn to that shame which, in shameful and manifest dangers, most destroys men. For to many, while they yet foresaw into what they were being carried, the so-called 'shame,' by the power of a seductive name, drew them on, overcome by the word, in fact to fall, with open eyes, into incurable misfortunes." That the historian neither himself shared in this meeting, being then present, nor heard the Athenians or Melians who made these speeches, is easy to learn from what he himself writes about himself in the book before this — that after his command at Amphipolis, driven out of his country, he spent all the rest of the war's time in Thrace. It remains, then, to consider whether he has composed the dialogue fitting to the matters and suitable to the persons who came together for the meeting, keeping as close as possible to the whole sense of what was truly said, as he himself foretold in the preface of his history. Were, then, the discourses about freedom — exhorting the Athenians not to enslave a Greek city that did them no wrong — proper and fitting to the Melians? And were the discourses about justice, in the same way, fitting to the Athenian generals — discourses that allow it neither to be examined nor spoken, but bring in the law of violence and greed, and declare that these things are just for the weak, whatever seems good to the stronger? For my part I do not think that these things are proper to be said by commanders sent out from the most law-abiding city to the cities abroad; nor would I think it right that the men of small cities, the Melians, who had shown no signal deed, should take more forethought for the honorable than for the safe and be ready to undergo all dreadful things that they might be compelled to do nothing unseemly, while the Athenians, who chose to abandon their land and city in the Persian War that they might submit to no shameful command, should accuse as fools those who chose the same things. And I think that, if any others had attempted to say these things in the presence of Athenians, the men who civilized the common life would have borne it grievously. I, then, for these reasons, do not praise this dialogue, comparing it with the other. For in that one Archidamus the Lacedaemonian both invites the Plataeans to just things and uses a style pure and clear and having no figure tortured or incoherent; but in this one the most prudent of the Greeks bring the most shameful reflections and embrace them in the most unpleasant style — unless indeed the historian, bearing a grudge against the city for his condemnation, has poured these reproaches upon it, from which all were bound to hate it. For what those who preside over cities and are entrusted with such great powers seem to think and say to the cities on behalf of their own country, all men suppose to be common to the city that sends them. And about the dialogues enough.

Of the public speeches, I have admired the one delivered at Athens in the first book by Pericles, about not yielding to the Lacedaemonians, the one that has this beginning: "Of my judgment, men of Athens, I always hold the same, not to yield to the Peloponnesians" — as both expressed divinely in its reflections, and as not troubling the ears either in the composition of the members or in the variation of incoherent and forced figures, but as having embraced all the virtues that arise about public speeches; and the speeches delivered by Nicias the general at Athens about the expedition to Sicily; and the letter sent by him to the Athenians, in which he asks for another and a successor force, being weak in body from disease; and the exhortation of the soldiers he made before the last sea-battle; and the consoling speech, when he was about to lead the army away on foot, having lost all the triremes; and any others there are of such public speeches, pure and clear and suited to the true contests. But above all those carried in the seven books I have admired the defense of the Plataeans, for nothing so much as that it is neither tortured nor over-studied, but adorned with a true and natural color. For the reflections are full of feeling and the style does not turn the ears away; and the composition is graceful and the figures proper to the matters. These, then, are the enviable works of Thucydides; and from these I propose to those writing history to take their models.

But the defense of Pericles in the second book, which he made on his own behalf, the Athenians being exasperated because he had persuaded them to take up the war, I do not praise whole; nor the public speeches about the city of the Mytileneans, which Cleon and Diodotus delivered, those in the third book; nor that of Hermocrates the Syracusan to the Camarinaeans; nor that of Euphemus the Athenian envoy, the speech opposite to it; nor those like these. For it is not necessary to enumerate all the speeches constructed in the same character of the dialect. But that no one may think I make assertions without proof, though I could furnish many proofs, I shall be content with two public speeches, that the discourse may not become long — the defense of Pericles and the accusation of Hermocrates to the Camarinaeans against the city of the Athenians.

Pericles, then, says this: "Both your anger toward me has come about as I expected — for I perceive the causes — and I have called the assembly for this reason, that I may remind and reproach, if in anything you are wrong either to be harsh with me or to yield to the misfortunes." These things, for Thucydides writing about the man in the historical figure, were proper; but for Pericles defending himself before an exasperated crowd they were not suitable to be said, and that at the beginning of the defense, before softening with some other words the angers of those who were reasonably distressed at their misfortunes — their best land cut up by the Lacedaemonians, much of the crowd lost in the plague, and the man himself having furnished the cause of these evils, the war which, persuaded by him, they took up. And the figure most suited to the thought was not this, the reproachful, but the deprecating; for it is not fitting for public speakers to provoke the angers of crowds, but to soften them. To these he adds a thought true indeed and forcefully expressed, but not useful to the present occasion: "For I think," he says, "that a city profits the private citizens more when it stands upright as a whole than when it prospers in each of its citizens severally but is brought down all together. For a man faring well in himself, his country being destroyed, perishes with it none the less; but one ill-fortuned in a fortunate city is far more saved." For if some of the citizens privately were harmed, but the commonwealth prospered, he spoke this well; but since all were in the uttermost misfortunes, no longer well. For neither did the hope about the future — that these dreadful things would turn out to the good of the city — have anything secure; for the future is unseen to man, and fortunes turn men's judgments about what is to be toward the present.

To these he adds a still more burdensome thought, and least suited to the present occasion: "And yet you are angry with such a man as I, who think myself inferior to none both in knowing what is needful and in expounding it, and a lover of my city and superior to money." For it would be wonderful if Pericles, the greatest of the orators of that time, was ignorant of what no one with moderate sense would have been ignorant of — that everywhere those who praise their own virtues unstintedly appear burdensome to their hearers, and most of all in contests before the courts and the assemblies, in which, that is, the danger to them is not about honors but about punishments. For then they are not only burdensome to others, but also unfortunate to themselves, calling out the envy of the many; and when a man has the same persons as judges and accusers, he needs countless tears and lamentations for this very thing first, to be heard with goodwill. But the demagogue is not content with these things, but works them out further and rephrases what was said: "For he who knows and does not teach it clearly is in the same case as if he had not thought it; and he who has both, but is ill-disposed to the city, would not similarly speak in a friendly manner; and if this too be present, and he be overcome by money, all these things together would be sold for this one." I do not know who would agree that, just as these things were true, so also it was fitting for Pericles to say them among Athenians exasperated against them. But it was not the invention of the best reflections and thoughts, by itself, that was worthy of effort, unless it should also be proper to the matters and to the persons and to the occasions and to all else. Rather, as I said at the outset, the historian, displaying his own judgment which he held about the virtue of Pericles, seems to have said these things out of place. He ought himself to declare whatever he wished about the man, but to render to the man in danger the humble and deprecating discourses that turn away anger; for this was fitting for a historian wishing to imitate the truth.

Wearisome too are those boyish embellishments of style and the complicated figures of the reflections: "to go to meet the enemy and ward them off not with high spirit only, but also with contempt. For high spirit is engendered even by a fortunate ignorance, and in a coward too; but contempt belongs to one who trusts that he excels his opponents in judgment also — which is the case with us. And intelligence, from an equal fortune, renders daring more secure by means of the over-confident; and it trusts less to hope, whose strength is in helplessness, and more to judgment from present resources, whose forethought is more secure." For these "high spirits" are rather frigid, and more proper to the manner of Gorgias; and the explanation of the words is both sophistical and tasteless; and "the daring which intelligence, from an equal fortune, renders more secure by means of the over-confident" has a revelation more obscure than the darknesses of Heraclitus; and "the strength of hope in helplessness" and "the more secure forethought of judgment from present resources" is too poetically periphrased. For he wishes to say that one ought to trust rather to the judgment we take from present things than to the hopes whose strength is in the future.

I have indeed reflected on this too: that while consoling the anger that had seized them over their present misfortunes — most of which befell them contrary to reckoning and unexpectedly — and exhorting them to bear their misfortunes nobly, not effacing the dignity of the city, but, having grieved out their private griefs, to lay hold of the common safety; and after this, having gone through how, holding the empire of the sea securely, they will be brought down neither by the king nor by the Lacedaemonians nor by any other nation of men (the proof of which was not the present but the future, and had its security not in forethought but in hopes) — then, forgetting these things, he thinks fit to bid them not trust the hope whose strength is in helplessness. For these things are contrary to one another, if indeed the painful thing had its perception already present, but the revelation of the benefit was still absent. But just as I do not praise these things, either in the matter of substance or in that of style, so I have admired those others as both exactly conceived and superbly expressed and pleasantly composed: "For to those to whom a choice has been given, prospering otherwise, it is much folly to make war; but if it was necessary either to yield at once and submit to one's neighbors or to prevail by running the risk, he who fled the danger is more to be blamed than he who stood it. And I am the same and do not change my ground; it is you who alter, since it has befallen you to have been persuaded while whole, but to repent while suffering." And still these: "For high spirit is enslaved by the sudden and the unexpected and what befalls with the greatest unreason . . . Yet, dwelling in a great city and reared in ways that match it, you ought to be willing to endure even misfortunes and not to efface your dignity. For men think it just, in equal measure, both to blame for failing of one's existing reputation whoever falls short through softness, and to hate for reaching after what does not belong to him whoever grasps in rashness." And still those things that rouse the souls of the Athenians toward their ancestral spirit, these: "It is likely too that you should help the city in the honor it has from empire, in which you all glory, and not flee its toils, or else not pursue its honors; nor think you are contending about one thing only, slavery instead of freedom, but also about the loss of empire and the danger of the hatreds you have incurred in your rule. From which you can no longer even withdraw, if anyone, fearing this too in the present, plays the good man through inactivity. For you now hold it as a tyranny, which to take seems unjust, but to let go is perilous." And the things like these — all that have moderate exchanges of words and figures, and are neither over-curious nor hard to follow.

From the public speech of Hermocrates I can praise these successes of the historian: "But we have not now come to declare, among those who know, how much the city of the Athenians wrongs — an easily accusable city; rather, much more to accuse ourselves, that, though we have the examples of the Greeks over there, how they were enslaved through not defending themselves, and now the same sophistries are present against us — settlements of Leontine kinsmen and aids of Egestaean allies — we are not willing, gathering together, to show them the more eagerly that these are not Ionians here, nor Hellespontines and islanders, who, ever changing their master, whether the Mede or some one man, are enslaved, but free Dorians, dwelling in Sicily from an independent Peloponnese. Or do we wait until each of us is taken city by city, knowing that in this way alone we are to be captured?" For these things, said in the clear and pure manner of the dialect, have taken on swiftness and beauty and tension and magnificence and force, and are full of contending feeling; things one might use both in a court and in assemblies and in conversing with friends. And besides these, those: "And if anyone envies or even fears — for the greater powers suffer both these things — and on account of them wishes Syracuse to be brought low, that we may be chastened, but to survive, for the sake of his own safety, he hopes for a wish beyond human power. For it is not possible for the same man to be at once the steward, alike, of his own desire and of fortune." And the things lying at the end of the speech: "We beg, then, and we call to witness, if we do not persuade you, that we are plotted against by Ionians, ever our enemies, and betrayed by you, Dorians by Dorians; and if the Athenians subdue us, they will prevail by your judgments, but be honored by their own name, and will take as the prize of victory no other than the one who furnished the victory." These things, then, and the like, I hold fine and worthy of emulation. But those others I do not know how I could praise: "For now they go to Sicily on a pretext, which you hear, but with an intent which we all suspect. And they seem to me to wish not to settle the Leontines, but rather to unsettle us." For the play on words is frigid and does not strike feeling, but study. And still those entangled figures that have many coils: "And so it was not for freedom, then, that either these of the Greeks or the Greeks resisted the Mede on their own behalf, but the one for enslaving us to themselves and not to him, the others for the change to a master not less intelligent but more ill-intelligent." And still the surfeit of the shifting from the plural to the singular and from speaking of persons to the person of the speaker: "And if it has occurred to anyone that the Syracusan, but not himself, is the enemy to the Athenian, and thinks it dreadful to run the risk on behalf of my land, let him reflect that he will be fighting in my land not for mine rather, but in equal measure for his own at the same time, and so much the more safely, in that, I not being destroyed beforehand, but having me as an ally, he will not contend deserted; and that the Athenian seeks not to chasten the enmity of the Syracusan." For these things are both boyish and over-curious and more obscure than the so-called riddles. And still these besides: "And if he err in judgment, having bewailed his own evils, he might perhaps one day wish again to envy my goods; but it is impossible for one who has thrown me away and not been willing to take on the same dangers — not about the names, but about the deeds." To which he adds an exclamation not fitting even for a boy: "For in word a man might save our power, but in deed his own safety."

There are also other things in this public speech worthy of blame, about which I have no need to say more; and I think I have made the matter sufficiently plain even through these — that of the style of Thucydides the best is that which has departed moderately from the customary and keeps the first and necessary virtues, and the worse is that which takes much turning aside from the common words and figures into the strange and forced and incoherent, on account of which not even any of the other virtues displays its own power. For this kind of expression is useful neither in the assemblies, in which the cities come together to deliberate about peace and war and the introduction of laws and the ordering of constitutions and the other common and great matters; nor in the courts, where the discourses are made, about death and exile and disfranchisement and bonds and the taking away of property, to those who have taken on the authority over these things ( . . . which distress the political crowd, not being accustomed to such hearings); nor in private conversations, in which we discuss the affairs of life with fellow-citizens or friends or kinsmen, narrating something of what has befallen us, or taking counsel about something necessary, or admonishing or exhorting or rejoicing with friends in their goods or grieving with them in their evils. For I forbear to say that not even their mothers and fathers would endure those who converse thus, because of the unpleasantness, but, as though hearing a foreign tongue, would need interpreters. These are the things of which I was persuaded about the historian, said with all truth according to my power.

It is necessary also to examine briefly the things some say in his favor, that I may not seem to have passed anything over. That this character is suited neither to political contests nor to private conversations, all will agree who are not corrupted in mind but have their perceptions in their natural state. But certain not undistinguished sophists undertake to say that this character is not suited to those prepared for crowded gatherings and pleading just causes, but that to those who bring out historical works — which need magnificence and dignity and the power to strike — it most of all befits to practice this expression, the glossarial and archaic and figurative, altered from the customary figures toward the strange and superfluous. For these writings, they say, are not constructed for market-place men, nor cobblers, nor handicraftsmen, nor the others who have not shared in a liberal upbringing, but for men who have come through the general studies to rhetoric and philosophy, to whom none of these things will appear strange. And some have undertaken to say that the historian wrote his histories thus, aiming not at those who would come after him, but at those of his own time, to whom this dialect . . . [was familiar]. [But it is] useful neither for the deliberative nor for the forensic contests, in which the men of the assembly and the jurors — not such as Thucydides supposed — come together.

To those, then, who think that to read and understand the dialect of Thucydides belongs to the well-educated alone, I have this to say: that they take away from the common life the necessary and useful thing for all (for nothing could be more necessary or more profitable), making it the possession of altogether few men — as in cities governed by oligarchy or tyranny; for easily counted are those able to put together all of Thucydides, and not even these without grammatical explanation in some places. And to those who refer the dialect of Thucydides to the ancient life, as though it were familiar to the men of that time, a brief and clear discourse suffices me: that of the many orators and philosophers who arose at Athens during the Peloponnesian War, none of them used this dialect, neither the orators around Andocides and Antiphon and Lysias, nor the Socratics around Critias and Antisthenes and Xenophon. From all these it is plain that the man was the first to have practiced this style of expression, that he might differ from the other historians. When, then, he uses it sparingly and moderately, he is wonderful and comparable to no other; but when he uses it to surfeit and tastelessly, neither marking off the occasions nor seeing the proper measure, he is to be blamed. I, for my part, would not think it right that historical writing be squalid and unadorned and commonplace, but that it should have something poetic too; nor wholly poetic, but having departed a little from what is customary; for surfeit is wearisome even of things very pleasant, while symmetry is everywhere useful.

One discourse still remains to me, the one about the orators and historians who imitated the man — necessary, like any other, to the completion of the subject, but causing me a certain hesitation and much caution, lest we furnish some occasion of slander to those accustomed to slander everything, foreign to the fairness we have used both about the discourses and about characters; to whom we shall perhaps seem to do a malicious and ill-natured thing, if we bring forward those who have not used imitation well and produce their writings, on which those men prided themselves most, and through which they acquired great wealth and were judged worthy of brilliant repute. But that no such suspicion may arise against us, the reproaching of any and the recalling of their faults we shall let pass; and about those who succeeded in imitation, adding a little, we shall there bring our discourse to an end. Of the ancient historians, then, as far as I know, no one became an imitator of Thucydides in these respects, in which he seems most of all to differ from the rest — in the glossarial and archaic and poetic and strange expression, and in the inverted and complicated thoughts that wish, by clipping, to signify many matters and take their resolutions at a long distance, and besides these, in the awkward figures that wander from the natural conjunction and have no place even in any poetry — from which the obscurity that ruins all that is fine and casts darkness over the virtues passed into discourse.

Of the orators, Demosthenes alone, just as of all the others who seemed to do something great and brilliant in discourse, so also became an emulator of Thucydides in many things, and added to his political speeches, taking from him, the virtues which neither Antiphon nor Lysias nor Isocrates, who held the first place among the orators of that time, possessed — I mean the swiftness and the compressions and the tensions and the bitterness and the compactness and the force that rouses the feelings; but the over-glossed and strange and poetic in the style, not thinking it suited to true contests, he left out, and neither did he love the wandering of figures from the natural sequence nor the solecistic appearance, but stayed in the customary, adorning his expression by changes and by variety and by bringing out no thought simply unfigured. But the complicated thoughts, signifying much in little and carrying their sequence at a long distance and bringing their reflections out of the unexpected, he emulated and added both to his deliberative and his forensic speeches, less in the private cases, but more lavishly in the public contests.

I shall set down examples from both — a few, though they are many, and sufficient for those who have read the man. There is a public speech of his having for its subject the war against the king, exhorting the Athenians not to take it up rashly, on the ground that neither is their own power a match for the king's, nor will the allied power lay hold of the dangers faithfully and securely; and he exhorts them, having prepared their own power, to be plain to the Greeks that they will undergo the danger on behalf of the freedom of all, if anyone goes against them; but before being prepared he does not allow them to send envoys to the Greeks to summon them to the war, as they would not obey. Taking this thought, he has constructed and figured it thus: "But then, if indeed you do what we now think you should, no one, surely, of all the Greeks is so high-minded in his own conceit that, seeing a thousand cavalry, and hoplites as many as one likes, and three hundred ships, he will not come and beg, thinking that with these he would most safely be saved. So that from summoning comes, even now, to beg, and to fail if you do not obtain; but from holding back while preparing your own affairs comes both to save those who beg, and to know well that all will come." These things have been altered from the political and familiar manner of expression of the many, and are better than the layman's; yet they have not been darkened, nor become obscure so as to need explanation. And having begun to speak about the preparation, he adds this: "But the first thing of the preparation, men of Athens, and the greatest, is for you to be so disposed in mind that each willingly and eagerly does whatever may be needed. For you see, men of Athens, that whatever you ever willed, and after that each thought it his own concern to act, never once escaped you; but whatever you willed, and after that looked to one another, as though each himself would not act, but his neighbor would do what was needful, never once came about for you." For here too the thought is complicated in a complicated way, yet it has been spoken so as to depart from commonness into the unfamiliar expression, while what is superfluous in it is kept within clarity. And in the greatest of the public speeches against Philip he has at once constructed the very beginning thus: "Many speeches being made, men of Athens, in well-nigh every assembly, about the wrongs Philip does, ever since he made the peace, not only to you but to the rest as well; and all, I know, would say, even if they do not do it, that one must both speak and act so that he may cease from his insolence and pay the penalty — yet I see all our affairs given up and let go to such a point that I fear to say a thing blasphemous, but true: if even all who came forward wished to speak, and you to vote, in such a way that things should be at their very worst, I do not think they could be worse disposed than now." Like to these are also those: "Then do you think that, if to those whom he did no harm, but who guarded perhaps against suffering it, he chooses rather to deceive than, forewarning, to use force, against you he will make war by forewarning, and that while you are willingly deceived?" And in the strongest of the forensic speeches, the one written on the Crown, having made mention of Philip's cleverness, by which he had outgeneraled the cities, he has figured the thought thus: "And I add no longer that of the cruelty which it is possible to see in those over whom Philip became master once for all, it befell others to make trial; but of the humanity which, throwing the rest of his affairs about himself, he feigned toward you, you, doing well, have reaped the fruits." And where he declares those who betrayed their affairs to Philip the cause of all the evils that befell the Greeks, he writes word for word thus: "And yet, by Heracles and all the gods, if one had to look at the truth, removing from the midst the lying and saying anything out of enmity — who in truth were they on whose head all men might reasonably and justly lay the cause of what has happened? You would find them to be the men like this one in each of the cities, not those like me; men who, when Philip's affairs were weak and altogether small, though we often forewarned and exhorted and taught the best things, for the sake of their own shameful gain gave up the common interest, deceiving and corrupting their fellow-citizens each in his own city, until they made them slaves."

I could bring countless examples from the speeches of Demosthenes, both the deliberative and the forensic, which have been constructed after the character of Thucydides — the one that has its variation in the common and familiar dialect. But that my discourse may not become longer than is needed, being content with these as sufficient to confirm what is proposed, I would not hesitate to lay it down for those who practice political discourse — those at least who still keep their judgments undistorted — that, using Demosthenes as their counselor, whom we are persuaded to have been the mightiest of all orators, they should imitate those constructions in which the brevity and the force and the strength and the tension and the magnificence and the virtues akin to these are plain to all men; but those that are riddling and hard to learn and need grammatical explanations and have much that is tortured and solecistic in their figurings, they should neither admire nor imitate. And to speak summarily, it has no reason that both should be equally worthy of emulation — both the things said unclearly by the historian and those that have taken on, along with the other virtues, clarity. We must rather agree that the more perfect things are better than the more imperfect, and the more manifest than the more obscure. What, then, have we learned, that we praise the whole dialect of the historian and force ourselves to say that Thucydides wrote these things for the men of his own time, as being familiar to all and known, but that of us who were to come after he took no account — we who cast out from the courts and the assemblies the whole style of Thucydides as useless? Rather we do not agree that the narrative part of it, except for a very few places, is wonderfully fine and well-fitted for all uses, but that the public-speaking part is not all suited to imitation, but only that part of it which is easy for all men to understand, though not possible for all to construct. I had things more pleasant than these to write to you about Thucydides, best Quintus Aelius Tubero — but not, indeed, truer.
